correctness.rationale: Since every E-class is represented, a new point has one definite old class and arbitrary adjacency bits only outside that class. Each allowable diagram is realized infinitely often, and homogeneity makes each diagram a single complete nonalgebraic type. Substituting z=w−1 in the graded polynomial recovers the exponent multiset directly, hence n and the part sizes. For scalar comparison at fixed n, the exponent sum (q−1)n and number q of summands are also fixed. Every representation of a binary integer comes from splitting its canonical bits by reversing carries. With at most four summands, split configurations with equal exponent-sum changes either agree or coincide as multisets (the only nontrivial two-source tie has consecutive source exponents). With five summands, one-bit split trees have depth sums 12, 13 and 14; two-bit trees have changes, after subtracting 3B, of 3d−8, 3d−9, 2d−7, d−7, −8 and −9, where d=A−B>0. All ties occur at d=1 or 2 and give the same leaf multisets. Four or five canonical bits give at most one representation per change. For three canonical bits, the only distinct tie is splitting B twice versus splitting A and C once when A+C=2B−1. Only the first multiset retains A. Their exponent sum is 5B−6=4n, yielding B=4t+2, n=5t+1. Subtraction from n gives exactly the two frozen profiles, positive precisely for 1≤d≤t−2; the canonical binary integer distinguishes all d, so every nonsingleton fibre has size exactly two. The unique first pair at n=16 gives T=53248. The cross-size example has T=320 and does not meet the fixed-n hypothesis.
residual_risks: Bounded exponent enumeration is not the completeness proof; the split classification establishes the all-size result. No collision classification for six or more classes or cross-size scalar reconstruction is inferred.

originality.rationale: The generic multipartite framework and the forward singleton-type formula are not credited as new. A neighboring record gives the analogous count with an extra new-class term and even a cross-class-count collision. The supported distinction is precise inverse recovery at fixed n and q: rigidity through four parts and the complete two-element collision families at five parts, derived from the equal-length, equal-first-moment binary representation problem. The inspected structural, additive and exact catalogue results do not give that classification.

value.rationale: Singleton types over a named set are a natural measure of what generic extension can distinguish. The theorem gives the exact information-loss boundary for the scalar under its intrinsic fixed-size constraint: four classes retain the unordered profile, while five have a unique first counterexample at size 16 and an exhaustive family for all larger sizes. The grading shows exactly how profile information is restored without suggesting recovery of invisible old graph edges. The classification goes well beyond reporting a first computed collision.
residual_risks: The use of all represented classes and fixed size is essential. The result does not classify the induced graph or recover the old cross-class edge matrix.
